a: to Cyrus
p: An early Christian letter quotes the Greek with 'Lord' (kyriō) for 'Cyrus' (Kyrō).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.plain: to Cyrus

readings.w: Epistle of Barnabas 12:11 (about AD 100–130), as first written in Codex Sinaiticus; not a manuscript of Isaiah
readings.plain: to the Lord

why: Every manuscript of Isaiah, Hebrew and Greek, names Cyrus, and 44:28 has already named him. The Barnabas reading is a one-letter change in a Christian quotation that makes the verse speak of Christ.
b: Barnabas reads: "The Lord said to Christ, my Lord, whose right hand I have held", and sets it beside Psalm 110:1. A later corrector of Sinaiticus restored 'Cyrus'. See the note on this verse.

a: the swelling hills
p: The Hebrew word is rare; the Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek have 'mountains'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QIsa-c (4Q57)
readings.plain: the swelling hills

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.plain: the mountains

why: Hadurim is unusual but not impossible (perhaps 'swellings', rises of ground); it is in 4QIsa-c as well, and the easier 'mountains' looks like a scribe's or translator's simplification. The meaning is the same.
b: The KJV, following the Hebrew, has 'make the crooked places straight'. 1QIsa-b has a third spelling, wehrurim, which is unclear. Many modern versions follow the scroll.

a: I make peace
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads 'good' for 'peace', making the pair 'good and evil'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QIsa-c (4Q57); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.plain: I make peace

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: I make good

why: Most witnesses read 'peace', and 'good' looks like a change to make the familiar pair 'good and evil'. The synagogue blessing based on the verse also says 'makes peace'.
b: The scroll's reading sharpens the theological question of the verse (see the note on 'create disaster').

a: I, the LORD, have created it.
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll ends the verse earlier and differs in several words.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC); 4QIsa-c (4Q57); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler) ('I am the Lord who created you')
readings.orig: יחד אני יהוה בראתיו (yachad 'ani YHWH bera'tiv)
readings.en: together. I, the LORD, have created it
readings.plain: I, the LORD, have created it.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)

why: Three other Qumran copies and the Greek have the line; the Great Isaiah Scroll probably lost it by a slip of the eye or shortened the verse.
b: The scroll also has 'Shout, heavens' (har'iu) for 'let it drip', 'who says to the earth' for 'let the earth open', and 'let salvation blossom' for 'bear fruit'.

a: every tongue will take its oath.
p: The Greek, followed by Paul, has 'every tongue will confess to God'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: every tongue will take its oath.

readings.w: the Greek (Ziegler, Rahlfs; Codex Alexandrinus and others); quoted in Romans 14:11 and Philippians 2:11
readings.en: every tongue will confess to God
readings.plain: every tongue will acknowledge God.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (Swete's text)
readings.en: every tongue will swear by God
readings.plain: every tongue will swear by God.

why: The Hebrew is the original; swearing by the LORD's name means acknowledging him as God (Deuteronomy 6:13; 19:18 below).
b: Paul quotes the 'confess' form in both letters. The Vaticanus reading agrees with the Hebrew and may have been corrected toward it. Compare 19:18 and 65:16, where swearing by the LORD marks loyalty.

a: the man who carries out my plan
p: The Hebrew is written 'his plan' (Ketiv) and read 'my plan' (Qere).

readings.w: Masoretic Text as read (Qere); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler) ('concerning what I have planned')
readings.plain: the man who carries out my plan

readings.w: Masoretic Text as written (Ketiv); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: the man who carries out his plan

why: The man is God's instrument (44:26; 46:10), and the read form fits the first person of the whole speech; the written form may be a scribal slip of waw for yod, letters easily confused.

a: I have chosen you
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads 'I have tested you', which fits the furnace image.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QIsa-d (4Q58) (damaged)
readings.plain: I have chosen you

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: I have tested you

readings.w: the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.plain: I have rescued you

why: The Hebrew 'chosen' is the harder reading (choosing in a furnace is unexpected), and the Aramaic sense 'test' is attested for bachar; 'tested' looks like an easier word. The NRSV and some others follow the scroll.

a: how could I let it be profaned?
t: How could it, or I, be profaned?
p: The Hebrew has no subject; two scrolls read 'how could I be profaned', the Greek 'my name is profaned'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: for how should it be profaned?
readings.plain: how could I let it be profaned?

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 4QIsa-d (4Q58)
readings.plain: how could I be profaned?

readings.w: the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.en: for my name is being profaned
readings.plain: for my name is being profaned.

why: The Hebrew's unstated subject is 'my name' (48:9); the scrolls make God the subject, the Greek names the name. All three mean the same.

a: Israel; through you I will win glory.
p: One medieval Hebrew manuscript lacks the word 'Israel'; every ancient witness has it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC); 4QIsa-d (4Q58); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.plain: Israel; through you I will win glory.

readings.w: Hebrew manuscript Kennicott 96 (medieval)
readings.plain: through you I will win glory.

why: Every scroll from Qumran and the Greek have the name, so its omission in a single late manuscript is almost certainly an accident. Scholars who think the servant is an individual sometimes delete 'Israel', but the evidence is against it.
b: See the note on this verse and the deep section on chapter 49.

a: so that Israel would be gathered to him.
p: The Hebrew is read lo 'to him' (Qere) but written lo' 'not' (Ketiv); the KJV follows 'not'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text as read (Qere); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.en: and Israel be gathered to him
readings.plain: so that Israel would be gathered to him.

readings.w: Masoretic Text as written (Ketiv); 4QIsa-d (4Q58); KJV
readings.plain: though Israel is not gathered.

why: The two words sound the same. 'To him' matches 'to bring Jacob back to him' in the line before; the Great Isaiah Scroll, 1QIsa-b and the Greek read it.
b: The KJV's 'Though Israel be not gathered, yet shall I be glorious' follows the written form, which 4QIsa-d also has.

a: the land of Syene
p: The Hebrew has 'Sinim'; the Great Isaiah Scroll has 'the Syenites', people of Aswan in southern Egypt.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: the land of Syene

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC); 4QIsa-d (4Q58)
readings.plain: the land of Sinim

readings.w: the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.en: from the land of the Persians
readings.plain: the land of the Persians

why: No land of Sinim is known. Syene, modern Aswan, was Egypt's southern frontier (Ezekiel 29:10; 30:6), and with 'north' and 'west' it completes the points of the compass. A Jewish garrison lived on Elephantine island at Syene in the 500s–400s BC, so the scroll's reading fits a real diaspora. Most modern versions follow it.
b: The KJV keeps 'Sinim'. Some older scholars, such as Gesenius, took Sinim as China, which is very unlikely for the time.

a: Can a tyrant's captives slip away?
t: A tyrant or a righteous man?
p: The Hebrew has 'a righteous man's captives'; the Great Isaiah Scroll has 'a tyrant's', as in 49:25.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); the Syriac and the Latin ('a strong man')
readings.plain: Can a tyrant's captives slip away?

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the captives of a righteous man
readings.plain: Can a righteous man's captives slip away?

readings.w: the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.plain: Can captives taken unjustly slip away?

why: The answer in 49:25 repeats the question's words, 'a warrior's captive' and 'the loot of a tyrant', which strongly supports 'tyrant' here. 'Righteous' may be a copying slip, or a scribe's thought that even 'lawful' captives would be freed.
b: The KJV has 'the lawful captive', following the Hebrew. Most modern versions follow the scroll.

a: I did not cover my face
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek read 'I did not turn my face away'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: I did not hide my face
readings.plain: I did not cover my face

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.en: I did not turn away my face
readings.plain: I did not turn my face away

why: Both readings say the servant faced his abusers. The Hebrew is the harder and more vivid reading; the other may come from 'I did not turn back' in 50:5.
b: In the first line the scroll also has a different, uncertain word for 'the floggers' (lemetilim). The Greek has 'I gave my back to whips and my cheeks to blows'.

a: the heavens will blow away like smoke
t: A line missing from the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the lines about heaven and earth wearing out.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.orig: כי שמים כעשן נמלחו והארץ כבגד תבלה
readings.en: for the heavens will vanish like smoke, and the earth wear out like a garment
readings.plain: the heavens will blow away like smoke

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: and see who created these

why: 1QIsa-b and the Greek have the lines. The Great Isaiah Scroll's 'and see who created these' copies 40:26, probably by a scribe whose eye skipped.
b: If the scroll's reading is chosen, the next line ('the earth wear thin like clothing') is also absent.

a: how can I comfort you?
t: "How can I comfort you?" or "Who will comfort you?"
p: The Hebrew has 'how (who) can I comfort you'; the scroll and the Greek read 'who will comfort you'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: who am I to comfort you? / how shall I comfort you?
readings.plain: how can I comfort you?

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler); the Syriac, the Targum and the Latin
readings.plain: who will comfort you?

why: The Hebrew's first person is harder and matches Lamentations 2:13 ('What can I compare to you, that I may comfort you?'). Many modern versions follow the other reading, which matches the question earlier in the verse.

a: and the God of Israel will guard your rear.
t: A line added in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The scroll adds 'he will be called the God of all the earth', from 54:5.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.en: and the God of Israel is your rear guard
readings.plain: and the God of Israel will guard your rear.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: and the God of Israel is your rear guard; he will be called the God of the whole earth
readings.plain: and the God of Israel will guard your rear; he will be called the God of the whole earth.

why: The added words are those of 54:5; a scribe has brought them in here. No other witness has them.

a: his look was so marred
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll adds one letter, which some read 'I anointed'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC); 4QIsa-c (4Q57)
readings.orig: כן משחת מאיש מראהו (ken mishchat me'ish mar'ehu)
readings.en: so marred beyond man was his appearance
readings.plain: his look was so marred

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: so I anointed his appearance beyond any man
readings.plain: I so anointed his look

why: The Hebrew 'disfigurement' fits the horror of the onlookers and 53:2–3. The scroll's extra yod may be only a spelling, though William Brownlee argued that the Qumran scribe read 'I anointed', a messianic reading.
b: The Greek has 'so your appearance will be without glory from men'.

a: Who has believed what we have heard?
p: The Greek begins with 'Lord', and John 12:38 and Romans 10:16 quote it that way.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC)
readings.plain: Who has believed what we have heard?

readings.w: the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler); quoted in John 12:38 and Romans 10:16
readings.orig: Κύριε, τίς ἐπίστευσεν τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν;
readings.en: Lord, who has believed our report?
readings.plain: Lord, who has believed what we have heard?

why: No Hebrew witness has 'Lord'; the Greek translator added an address to make the verse a prayer.

a: because my people rebelled
p: Two Qumran scrolls read 'his people'; the Hebrew, 4QIsa-d and the Greek read 'my people'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QIsa-d (4Q58); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler) (τοῦ λαοῦ μου)
readings.en: for the rebellion of my people
readings.plain: because my people rebelled

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC)
readings.en: for the rebellion of his people
readings.plain: because his people rebelled

why: The oldest Greek and one Qumran copy agree with the Hebrew. The two letters waw and yod were easily confused at Qumran, so the scrolls' 'his people' may be a copying change; it could also be original, with the speakers (53:1–10) speaking of the servant's own people.
b: The reading matters for the identity question. With 'my people', God or the prophet speaks of Israel, and the servant suffers for Israel's sin, which Origen used against the reading of the servant as Israel. With 'his people', the servant suffers for his own people's sins. See the notes on this verse.

a: a rich man in his death
p: The Hebrew has 'in his deaths' (plural); the Great Isaiah Scroll has 'rich men' and 'his death', or 'his tomb'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC)
readings.en: and with a rich man in his deaths
readings.plain: a rich man in his death

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: and with rich men his tomb (or: in his death)
readings.plain: rich men in his death

readings.w: the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.orig: καὶ τοὺς πλουσίους ἀντὶ τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and (I will give) the rich for his death
readings.plain: the rich in exchange for his death

why: The Hebrew plural 'deaths' is probably an intensive plural, 'his violent death', as in Ezekiel 28:10, and the Plain renders it as a singular. Ibn Ezra noted the plural; some interpreters read it as the many deaths of a people. The scroll's bwmtw may be 'in his death' with a different spelling, or bamato, 'his burial mound', a reading some scholars prefer.
b: The scroll also reads 'they gave' (plural) where the Hebrew has 'he (one) gave'; the Plain already says 'They gave'. The Greek makes God the subject: 'I will give the wicked for his burial and the rich for his death'.

a: and made him sick
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads 'and he pierced him'; the Greek has 'to cleanse him from the blow'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC); 4QIsa-d (4Q58)
readings.plain: and made him sick

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.plain: and pierced him

readings.w: the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.en: to cleanse him from the blow
readings.plain: and to cleanse him from the blow

why: Two other Qumran copies agree with the Hebrew, which ties the verse to 'sickness' in 53:3–4. The scroll's verb is the one in 53:5, 'pierced', probably brought in from there.
b: The Greek continues: 'if you give an offering for sin, your soul will see a long-lived offspring', making the hearers the subject.

a: he will see light
p: Three Qumran scrolls and the Greek add 'light'; the Hebrew has only 'he will see'.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC); 4QIsa-d (4Q58) (damaged, restored by its editors); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler) (φῶς)
readings.plain: he will see light

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: he will see it

why: 'He will see' has no object in the Hebrew, which is awkward. The word 'light' in two independent Qumran scrolls and the Greek suggests it fell out of the Masoretic line. 'Seeing light' means coming alive again (Job 33:28, 30; Psalm 36:9). Most modern versions follow it; the KJV ('He shall see of the travail of his soul') does not.
b: The Great Isaiah Scroll also reads 'and by his knowledge' and 'his servant'. The Greek reads 'to show him light and to form him with understanding'.

a: He bore the sin of many
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll, 4QIsa-d and the Greek have the plural 'sins of many'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: He bore the sin of many

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 4QIsa-d (4Q58); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.plain: He bore the sins of many

why: The meaning is the same: the singular is collective. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, which is also the form Hebrews 9:28 renders with a plural.

a: and he will step in for the rebels.
t: For the rebels, or for their rebellions?
p: Two Qumran scrolls read 'for their rebellions'; the Greek has 'because of their iniquities he was handed over'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QIsa-b (4Q56)
readings.en: and for the transgressors he will intercede
readings.plain: and he will step in for the rebels.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, first century BC)
readings.en: and for their transgressions he will intercede
readings.plain: and he will step in for their rebellions.

readings.w: the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.orig: καὶ διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας αὐτῶν παρεδόθη
readings.en: and because of their sins he was handed over
readings.plain: and was handed over because of their sins.

why: The Hebrew 'rebels' repeats the word of the line before ('counted with the rebels'); 4QIsa-b agrees with it.
b: The Greek 'handed over' (paredothē), used twice in 53:12 and in 53:6, is the verb of Romans 4:25 ('handed over for our trespasses').

a: the waters of Noah
p: Many Hebrew manuscripts and the Latin read 'the days of Noah'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QIsa-c (4Q57) and 4QIsa-d (4Q58); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.plain: the waters of Noah

readings.w: many medieval Hebrew manuscripts; Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) (written as one word); the Latin (sicut in diebus Noe)
readings.plain: the days of Noah

why: The same consonants can be divided as 'for the waters of' or 'like the days of'. 'Waters' matches 'Noah's waters' in the next line.

a: and your children's peace will be great.
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll writes 'your builders' in the second line, the very reading the Talmud plays on.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4QIsa-c (4Q57); the Greek (Septuagint; Ziegler)
readings.en: and great will be the peace of your children
readings.plain: and your children's peace will be great.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: and great will be the peace of your builders
readings.plain: and your builders' peace will be great.

why: Most witnesses repeat 'your children' from the first line; the scroll's 'builders' fits 54:11–12 and may be an old interpretive reading.
b: The Talmud says: 'Do not read banayikh, your children, but bonayikh, your builders' (Berakhot 64a): Torah scholars build the world's peace. The scroll shows the reading existed centuries earlier.
